titre: English Language GCE O Level Paper 1 – Original Paper No. 1

exercices.enonce_intro_markdown: **Paper 1 - Multiple choice (1 hour 30 minutes).** Answer ALL 50 questions. All questions carry equal marks (1 mark each). Each question has four suggested answers A, B, C and D: choose only one answer for each question. The paper has four sections: A listening comprehension (questions 1 to 10), B reading comprehension (questions 11 to 25), C grammar (questions 26 to 40) and D vocabulary (questions 41 to 50).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Listening passage.** In the real examination the examiner reads this passage aloud once. Read it once, then answer questions 1 to 10.

**A Talk and a Story**

**Section One**

Good morning, class. I want to talk to you about money, because the long holidays are near and many of you will help in your parents' shops or sell small things by the roadside. Saving is not about how much you earn. A boy who earns five hundred francs a day and keeps one hundred of it will have more at the end of the month than a boy who earns two thousand francs and spends it all by evening. The first rule is to decide, before you receive the money, how much you will set aside. The second rule is to keep that part where you cannot reach it easily. A small tin under the bed is too easy to open, so ask a trusted adult or a savings group to keep it for you. The third rule is to write down what you spend, because most people are surprised to learn where their money goes. Finally, remember that saving is a habit. Begin with a small amount and be faithful to it; the habit matters more than the first sum.

**Section Two**

Tabe sold roasted groundnuts at the bus park in Bafoussam. One Saturday, a tired traveller bought a small bag, paid with a ten-thousand-franc note and hurried to catch his bus before Tabe could give him his change. Tabe ran after him, calling, but the engine roared and the bus pulled away. He stood for a long time with the note in his hand and the smell of diesel in his nose. Ten thousand francs was more than he earned in a week. A voice inside him whispered, "Nobody saw. Keep it." Yet when he reached home, his grandmother noticed that he ate nothing. "Something is troubling you more than hunger," she said. Tabe told her everything.

**Section Three**

On the next market day, Tabe's grandmother sent him to the bus park with the note folded in his pocket. Every Saturday for a month he looked for the traveller, who never came. In the fifth week the same man stepped off a bus, looking tired and worried, and was surprised to see the boy running towards him. "You left this with me," said Tabe, holding out the note. The man stared at him, then at the note, and finally laughed with relief. He pushed two thousand francs into Tabe's hand and ordered ten bags of groundnuts for his family. From that day he stopped at Tabe's tray each time he passed through the town, and other travellers, hearing the story, did the same. Tabe's tray was never empty again.

**Questions 1 to 4 (Section One)**

In this talk, the speaker is mainly advising the students on \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
In a listening test, read the question first, then follow the speaker's words: the right option says what was said or what the words clearly suggest, never what merely sounds likely in real life.

The talk opens with the holidays and money, then insists that saving is not about how much you earn and gives three rules for keeping part of what you receive. The advice is therefore about keeping money, not about earning more or asking for more.

**In the passage:** "Saving is not about how much you earn."

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
Earning more or selling things by the roadside is mentioned only as the situation of the students, not as the advice given.

choix.texte: how to keep part of the money they receive
how to open a small shop by the roadside
how to earn more money during the holidays
how to ask adults for pocket money

In a listening test, read the question first, then follow the speaker's words: the right option says what was said or what the words clearly suggest, never what merely sounds likely in real life.

The speaker compares two boys: one earns five hundred francs a day and keeps one hundred of it, the other earns two thousand francs and spends it all by evening. The first boy ends the month with more because he keeps part of his earnings.

To find the meaning of a word in context, read the sentence around it, test each option in place of the word, and keep the one that fits both the meaning and the grammar of the sentence.

The speaker is talking about the habit of saving: begin with a small amount and be faithful to it, because the habit matters more than the first sum. To be faithful to the habit is to keep on doing it.

questions.enonce_markdown: (Listening passage in question 1, Section Three) The man was surprised to see Tabe running towards him. This suggests that the man \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
In a listening test, read the question first, then follow the speaker's words: the right option says what was said or what the words clearly suggest, never what merely sounds likely in real life.

Surprise comes from the unexpected. Tabe had looked for him for four weeks and he never came, so the man had no reason to think the boy was waiting with his note; he did not expect to meet Tabe again.

**In the passage:** "was surprised to see the boy running towards him"

questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
In a listening test, read the question first, then follow the speaker's words: the right option says what was said or what the words clearly suggest, never what merely sounds likely in real life.

Tabe resisted the temptation to keep the note and returned it. The man rewarded him and sent customers his way, so his tray was never empty again. The story teaches that honest behaviour is rewarded for a long time.

**In the passage:** "Tabe's tray was never empty again."

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
The first wrong option is a detail of the story, not its lesson, and the last one is contradicted by the ending.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Read the passage below carefully and answer questions 11 to 25.**

**The Day the Bridge Went Down**

(1) By the time the last bell rang that Thursday, the sky over Wum had turned the colour of a wet slate. Teacher Ayuk warned us to go straight home, but my sister Ma'a, who was nine and believed that rules were for other children, insisted on stopping to buy roasted plantain at Mami Beri's stall. By the time we left the junction, the first drops were already as heavy as pebbles.

(2) Our house stands on the far side of the Mbah stream, which on ordinary days is a cheerful trickle that a goat can cross without wetting its belly. We reached it to find a different creature altogether. The water had swollen to the colour of strong tea and growled between its banks like an old man refusing to share his seat. The wooden footbridge, three planks tied with creeper, shivered under the current. I held Ma'a's hand and stepped forward, only to hear a crack like a gunshot. The middle plank snapped, and the whole bridge folded quietly into the water as though it had been waiting for permission.

(3) We stood frozen. Ma'a, to my surprise, said nothing; she only squeezed my hand until my fingers went numb. Then, through the rain, I heard someone laughing. It was Pa Nkeng, our neighbour, who had retired from the council seven years before and who, according to my mother, had opinions on everything and a solution to none. He was sitting under a plastic sheet on the opposite bank, calmly eating groundnuts.

(4) "You children have chosen a fine afternoon for a swim," he shouted. "Do not move! The water will not wait for you, but it will be gone by dusk. Walk up the bank to the fallen kola tree. It has been there since the wind of March and has never been of any use to anyone. Today it will be." I did not trust a man who joked while we were in danger, but I had no better idea. We climbed the bank with the mud sucking at our shoes, found the huge trunk lying across the stream like a bridge built by a careless giant, and crossed on hands and knees, with Ma'a in front, muttering a prayer in two languages.

(5) When we reached the other side, Pa Nkeng handed each of us a handful of groundnuts as if we had come back from a festival. "Tell your mother," he said, "that the council will repair that bridge about the time the mango trees learn to sing." Then he laughed again, louder this time, and I realised that the man who made jokes in a storm had been more worried than he had let us see: his hands, I noticed, were shaking.

(6) At home my mother scolded us for being late, then hugged us until I could hardly breathe. That night, with the rain drumming on the zinc roof, Ma'a whispered from her mat, "Next time, I will buy my plantain on a dry day." I lay awake smiling at the sentence, and at the memory of a kola tree that had waited three months to be useful.

**Questions 11 to 25**

The narrator and his sister reached home late because \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
In a reading comprehension question about a detail, find the sentence in the passage that answers it and compare each option with that sentence word for word; the correct option is the one the text supports.

Paragraph 1 says that Ma'a insisted on stopping to buy roasted plantain at a stall, although the teacher had told the pupils to go straight home.

**In the passage:** "insisted on stopping to buy roasted plantain"

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
The teacher actually told them to go home straight away, and the bridge falls later in the passage.

choix.texte: Ma'a insisted on stopping to buy plantain
the bridge had already fallen when they left school
their teacher kept them back in class
they lost their way in the rain

questions.enonce_markdown: (Reading passage, questions 11 to 25) In paragraph 2, the stream is said to growl "like an old man refusing to share his seat". This comparison is a \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A simile compares two things using like or as, a metaphor states that one thing is another, and an oxymoron joins two opposite ideas; name the device by looking at the exact words used.

The comparison uses the word like to link the growling stream with an old man, so it is a simile. A metaphor would say that the stream was an old man, with no link word.

**In the passage:** "like an old man refusing to share his seat"

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
Many learners call every comparison a metaphor; the word like is the sign of a simile.

### Conseil
Look for like or as before you decide on the device.

questions.enonce_markdown: (Reading passage, questions 11 to 25) In paragraph 2, the words "folded quietly into the water" suggest that the bridge \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
To find the meaning of a word in context, read the sentence around it, test each option in place of the word, and keep the one that fits both the meaning and the grammar of the sentence.

To fold is to bend and give way, and quietly adds that nothing resisted. The bridge gave way without any struggle, as if it had been waiting for permission.

**In the passage:** "folded quietly into the water"

**Answer: A.**

Folded and floated are both soft words, but only folded suggests collapse.

questions.enonce_markdown: (Reading passage, questions 11 to 25) The word "calmly" in paragraph 3 is used as a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A word class is decided by the job the word does in its sentence: a word that tells how, when or where an action happens is an adverb, and one that describes a noun is an adjective.

Calmly describes how Pa Nkeng was eating, so it modifies the verb and is an adverb. The ending -ly is a clue, though the job of the word is what decides.

**In the passage:** "calmly eating groundnuts"

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Reading passage, questions 11 to 25) Pa Nkeng says that the council will repair the bridge "about the time the mango trees learn to sing". This means that the repair \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
An inference question asks what the passage suggests without stating it: collect the clues in the text, then choose the option that all the clues support and that no sentence contradicts.

Mango trees cannot learn to sing, so the time he names will never come. Pa Nkeng is saying, with a joke, that the council will not repair the bridge.

**In the passage:** "about the time the mango trees learn to sing"

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
A time-word such as season misleads: the phrase belongs to a joke about something impossible.

### Conseil
When a speaker names an impossible event as the time, he means never.

choix.texte: will be done by the villagers
will be finished by the evening
will start in the mango season

questions.enonce_markdown: (Reading passage, questions 11 to 25) The narrator realised that Pa Nkeng had been worried because \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
An inference question asks what the passage suggests without stating it: collect the clues in the text, then choose the option that all the clues support and that no sentence contradicts.

The narrator says that the man who made jokes in a storm had been more worried than he had let them see, and he gives the proof: the man's hands were shaking.

**In the passage:** "his hands, I noticed, were shaking"

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
He actually laughed again, louder, and the food was a handful of groundnuts; neither shows worry.

questions.enonce_markdown: (Reading passage, questions 11 to 25) Which of the following best describes the writer's attitude throughout the passage?
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
An inference question asks what the passage suggests without stating it: collect the clues in the text, then choose the option that all the clues support and that no sentence contradicts.

The writer uses jokes, comparisons and Pa Nkeng's humour throughout, yet the danger at the stream and the shaking hands show real concern. The tone is light-hearted but touched with concern.

**Answer: D.**

### Piège à éviter
The danger could suggest a gloomy tone, but the humour of the narration and the happy ending rule it out.

rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: An inference question asks what the passage suggests without stating it: collect the clues in the text, then choose the option that all the clues support and that no sentence contradicts.

questions.enonce_markdown: (Reading passage, questions 11 to 25) Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
In a reading comprehension question about a detail, find the sentence in the passage that answers it and compare each option with that sentence word for word; the correct option is the one the text supports.

A good title covers the whole passage: the bridge falls, and a tree that had been of no use to anyone saves the children. The first option names both the tree and the bridge.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
The council, the groundnuts and swimming are small details or events that never happen.

choix.texte: The Day an Idle Tree Became a Bridge
How Pa Nkeng Lost His Groundnuts
A Meeting of the Village Council

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section C - Grammar.** For questions 26 to 40, choose the best answer to complete each sentence.

My cousin \_\_\_\_\_\_ in Douala since he left school.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Choose the verb form from the time words in the sentence: since and for with a situation that continues up to now need the present perfect, a finished past time needs the simple past.

Since he left school marks a period that began in the past and still continues, so the present perfect has lived is needed.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
The simple past lived would suit a finished time such as last year, but since points to the present.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Verb tenses
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Choose the verb form from the time words in the sentence: since and for with a situation that continues up to now need the present perfect, a finished past time needs the simple past.

questions.enonce_markdown: Unless you \_\_\_\_\_\_ your homework, the teacher will not let you go out.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
After unless, if not or when a future result is promised, the verb in the condition stays in the present tense, while the result clause uses will or can.

After unless, the verb stays in the present tense, and the result clause carries will: Unless you finish your homework, the teacher will not let you go out.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
Will after unless is a common slip: the future is expressed in the result clause only.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Conditionals: choosing the verb pattern after if and after Had
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: After unless, if not or when a future result is promised, the verb in the condition stays in the present tense, while the result clause uses will or can.

questions.enonce_markdown: The prize was shared between Ebot and \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
After a preposition or a verb, use the object pronoun (me, him, her, us, them); use the subject pronoun (I, he, she, we, they) only when the pronoun is the subject of a verb.

After the preposition between, the object pronoun is needed, so the sentence is: The prize was shared between Ebot and me.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
Many learners think that I sounds more polite; it is correct only as the subject of a verb.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Pronouns: choosing the right word for the person or thing
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: After a preposition or a verb, use the object pronoun (me, him, her, us, them); use the subject pronoun (I, he, she, we, they) only when the pronoun is the subject of a verb.

questions.enonce_markdown: The list of required books \_\_\_\_\_\_ pinned on the notice board.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
The verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not with the noun nearest to it: in a phrase like the list of books, the head noun is list.

The head noun of the subject is list, which is singular, so the verb is singular: The list of required books is pinned on the notice board.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
The nearest noun, books, is plural and pulls the verb towards are, but it is only part of the phrase that describes the list.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Subject-verb agreement
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: The verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not with the noun nearest to it: in a phrase like the list of books, the head noun is list.

questions.enonce_markdown: The little girl is allergic \_\_\_\_\_\_ groundnut oil.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Many adjectives and verbs keep one fixed preposition (allergic to, good at, afraid of); learn them as pairs because no rule gives the right choice.

The adjective allergic keeps the preposition to: allergic to groundnut oil.

**Answer: B.**

rappels_de_methode.competence: Prepositions: time, place and the words that need a fixed partner
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Many adjectives and verbs keep one fixed preposition (allergic to, good at, afraid of); learn them as pairs because no rule gives the right choice.

questions.enonce_markdown: The match went on \_\_\_\_\_\_ the heavy rain.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A connector must fit the logic of the two ideas it joins: although and in spite of introduce a contrast, because and since give a cause, so introduces a result.

The idea is a contrast: the rain could have stopped the match, but it did not. In spite of introduces that contrast, while the other options give a cause or a replacement.

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
Because of and owing to give a cause, which would mean that the rain made the match continue.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Connectors: linking ideas with the right word
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: A connector must fit the logic of the two ideas it joins: although and in spite of introduce a contrast, because and since give a cause, so introduces a result.

questions.enonce_markdown: The pupils listened \_\_\_\_\_\_ to the headmaster's warning.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
An adverb of manner modifies a verb and usually ends in -ly; an adjective cannot do this job, and a noun cannot either.

The word describes how the pupils listened, so an adverb is needed: attentively.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
Attentive is an adjective and can describe the pupils, but it cannot describe the verb listened.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Adverbs: choosing the right kind and putting it in the right place
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: An adverb of manner modifies a verb and usually ends in -ly; an adjective cannot do this job, and a noun cannot either.

questions.enonce_markdown: Let's wait for the others, \_\_\_\_\_\_?
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A question tag repeats the auxiliary of the statement with the opposite polarity; the fixed forms are let's... shall we and the imperative... will you.

The statement begins with Let's, and the fixed tag for it is shall we.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
Learners often build the tag from the apparent verb, giving don't we, but let's has its own tag.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Question Tags: matching the tag to the statement
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: A question tag repeats the auxiliary of the statement with the opposite polarity; the fixed forms are let's... shall we and the imperative... will you.

questions.enonce_markdown: "I will bring the books tomorrow," said Ndi. Ndi said that he \_\_\_\_\_\_ the books the next day.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
When direct speech becomes reported speech after a past reporting verb, the tense moves back (will becomes would, can becomes could) and time words change (tomorrow becomes the next day).

The reporting verb said is in the past, so will moves back to would, and tomorrow becomes the next day: Ndi said that he would bring the books the next day.

**Answer: D.**

### Piège à éviter
Keeping will is a common slip; had brought would change the meaning to an earlier time.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Reported speech
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: When direct speech becomes reported speech after a past reporting verb, the tense moves back (will becomes would, can becomes could) and time words change (tomorrow becomes the next day).

questions.enonce_markdown: The cook is preparing the meal. In the passive, this becomes: The meal \_\_\_\_\_\_ by the cook.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
To make a passive sentence, move the object to the subject position and use the matching form of be with the past participle; the tense of be stays the tense of the active verb.

The active verb is in the present continuous, so the passive uses the present continuous of be with the past participle: is being prepared.

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
Is prepared drops the continuous idea, and the other two options change the tense.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Passive voice
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: To make a passive sentence, move the object to the subject position and use the matching form of be with the past participle; the tense of be stays the tense of the active verb.

questions.enonce_markdown: The \_\_\_\_\_\_ playground is next to the church.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A plural noun that does not end in -s takes 's to show ownership (children's), whereas a regular plural takes only the apostrophe (girls').

Children is already plural without -s, so ownership is shown with 's: the children's playground.

**Answer: D.**

### Piège à éviter
Childrens' treats the word as if it were a regular plural; there is no -s to follow.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Possessives: choosing between my, mine, Ngo's and the girls'
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: A plural noun that does not end in -s takes 's to show ownership (children's), whereas a regular plural takes only the apostrophe (girls').

questions.enonce_markdown: She wore a \_\_\_\_\_\_ dress to the wedding.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Adjectives before a noun follow a fixed order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, then the noun.

The order is opinion (beautiful), size (long), colour (red) and material (cotton), then the noun: a beautiful long red cotton dress.

**Answer: D.**

### Piège à éviter
The other options put colour or material too early.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Adjective Order: building the noun phrase in the right sequence
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Adjectives before a noun follow a fixed order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, then the noun.

questions.enonce_markdown: The police arrested the \_\_\_\_\_\_ at dawn.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Nouns ending in -f or -fe often change to -ves in the plural (thief, thieves); learn the common exceptions and irregular plurals one by one.

Thief ends in -f, which changes to -v before -es in the plural: thieves.

**Answer: B.**

rappels_de_methode.competence: Plural Nouns: regular, irregular and compound forms
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Nouns ending in -f or -fe often change to -ves in the plural (thief, thieves); learn the common exceptions and irregular plurals one by one.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A relative clause that only adds extra information is closed off with commas on both sides; a clause that identifies the noun takes no commas.

The clause who lives in Kumba only adds extra information about my sister, so it is closed off by a comma before and a comma after.

**Answer: D.**

### Piège à éviter
Each wrong option leaves out one of the two commas or puts a comma in the wrong place.

### Conseil
Read the sentence aloud: the pauses fall where the commas belong.

choix.texte: My sister who lives in Kumba, is a nurse.
My sister, who lives in Kumba is a nurse.
My sister who, lives in Kumba, is a nurse.
My sister, who lives in Kumba, is a nurse.

themes: O Level English - spelling and punctuation

rappels_de_methode.competence: Spelling and Punctuation: getting the small details right
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: A relative clause that only adds extra information is closed off with commas on both sides; a clause that identifies the noun takes no commas.

questions.enonce_markdown: The meeting was \_\_\_\_\_\_ because of the strike.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle with a new meaning: called off means cancelled, while the same verb with another particle means something different.

To call off an event is to cancel it, which is what a strike would cause: The meeting was called off because of the strike.

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
Called on and called up exist but mean to visit someone and to summon, and called at means to stop at a place.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Phrasal verbs
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle with a new meaning: called off means cancelled, while the same verb with another particle means something different.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section D - Vocabulary.** For questions 41 to 46, choose the answer that best completes each sentence.

The headmaster \_\_\_\_\_\_ the pupils for their excellent results.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
For a vocabulary question, test each option in the sentence for meaning and for the words it normally keeps company with, and drop options that are close in sound but different in meaning.

To commend is to praise, which suits excellent results: The headmaster commended the pupils for their excellent results.

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
Condemned, commanded and commenced look like commended but mean to blame, to order and to begin.
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

rappels_de_methode.competence: Vocabulary in Context: working out meaning from clues
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: For a vocabulary question, test each option in the sentence for meaning and for the words it normally keeps company with, and drop options that are close in sound but different in meaning.

questions.enonce_markdown: The thief managed to \_\_\_\_\_\_ the police by hiding among the market stalls.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
For a vocabulary question, test each option in the sentence for meaning and for the words it normally keeps company with, and drop options that are close in sound but different in meaning.

To evade someone is to escape from them cleverly, which is what hiding from the police does.

**Answer: D.**

### Piège à éviter
Invade is close in spelling but means to enter by force, and evacuate means to leave a place.
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

rappels_de_methode.competence: Vocabulary in Context: working out meaning from clues
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: For a vocabulary question, test each option in the sentence for meaning and for the words it normally keeps company with, and drop options that are close in sound but different in meaning.

questions.enonce_markdown: The long drought had a serious \_\_\_\_\_\_ on the maize harvest.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Affect is a verb meaning to influence; effect is a noun meaning a result; many pairs of similar words differ in their word class as well as in their meaning.

After the article a and the adjective serious, a noun is needed, and the noun meaning a result is effect.

**Answer: D.**

### Piège à éviter
Affect is a verb, so it cannot follow a serious in this sentence.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Confusable words
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Affect is a verb meaning to influence; effect is a noun meaning a result; many pairs of similar words differ in their word class as well as in their meaning.

questions.enonce_markdown: The old man was too \_\_\_\_\_\_ to climb the steep hill without a stick.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
For a vocabulary question, test each option in the sentence for meaning and for the words it normally keeps company with, and drop options that are close in sound but different in meaning.

Frail describes a weak person, which fits a man who needs a stick for a steep hill.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
Flimsy describes objects that break easily, and rigid and stubborn do not explain the need for a stick.
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

rappels_de_methode.competence: Vocabulary in Context: working out meaning from clues
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: For a vocabulary question, test each option in the sentence for meaning and for the words it normally keeps company with, and drop options that are close in sound but different in meaning.

questions.enonce_markdown: Her kind\_\_\_\_\_\_ to strangers is known all over the village.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A suffix changes the word class of a base word: -ness turns an adjective into a noun (kind, kindness), while -ity, -ment and -ance attach to other kinds of base.

The sentence needs a noun made from the adjective kind, and the suffix that does this is -ness: kindness.

**Answer: D.**

### Piège à éviter
The suffixes -ity, -ment and -ance form nouns from other bases and do not fit kind.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Word Formation: prefixes, suffixes and finishing the word
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: A suffix changes the word class of a base word: -ness turns an adjective into a noun (kind, kindness), while -ity, -ment and -ance attach to other kinds of base.

questions.enonce_markdown: When the manager said that he was "under the weather", he meant that he was \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
An idiom has a fixed meaning that cannot be read word for word; learn it with its meaning and test the options against what the speaker actually says.

The idiom under the weather means to feel unwell, so the manager was saying that he was ill.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
The words suggest rain, but an idiom must be read as a whole and not word for word.
themes: O Level English - idioms and proverbs

rappels_de_methode.competence: Idioms and proverbs
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: An idiom has a fixed meaning that cannot be read word for word; learn it with its meaning and test the options against what the speaker actually says.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**For questions 47 and 48, choose the answer that best explains the meaning of the word in bold.**

The farmer was **reluctant** to sell his land.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A synonym replaces the word without changing the meaning of the sentence; test each option in the sentence and eliminate the ones that change the meaning.

Reluctant means not willing to do something, so unwilling keeps the meaning of the sentence.

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
Eager is the opposite, and afraid and forced change the meaning.
themes: O Level English - synonyms and antonyms
O Level English - vocabulary in context

rappels_de_methode.competence: Synonyms and Antonyms: choosing words of similar or opposite meaning
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: A synonym replaces the word without changing the meaning of the sentence; test each option in the sentence and eliminate the ones that change the meaning.

questions.enonce_markdown: The lawyer gave a **concise** summary of the case.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A synonym replaces the word without changing the meaning of the sentence; test each option in the sentence and eliminate the ones that change the meaning.

A concise summary says much in few words, so short and clear is the closest meaning.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
Long and detailed is the opposite of concise.
themes: O Level English - synonyms and antonyms
O Level English - vocabulary in context

rappels_de_methode.competence: Synonyms and Antonyms: choosing words of similar or opposite meaning
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: A synonym replaces the word without changing the meaning of the sentence; test each option in the sentence and eliminate the ones that change the meaning.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**For questions 49 and 50, choose the answer that gives the opposite of the word in bold.**

The river is very **shallow** at this point.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
An antonym is the word with the opposite meaning in the same context: first define the word in bold, then pick the option that says the reverse.

Shallow means not deep, so the opposite is deep.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
Narrow and wide describe breadth, not depth, so they cannot be the opposite of shallow.
themes: O Level English - synonyms and antonyms

rappels_de_methode.competence: Synonyms and Antonyms: choosing words of similar or opposite meaning
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: An antonym is the word with the opposite meaning in the same context: first define the word in bold, then pick the option that says the reverse.

questions.enonce_markdown: The manager's answer was **ambiguous**.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
An antonym is the word with the opposite meaning in the same context: first define the word in bold, then pick the option that says the reverse.

Ambiguous means open to more than one meaning, so the opposite is clear: an answer that can be read only one way.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
Polite, short and rude describe the manner or the length of an answer, not whether its meaning is clear.

### Conseil
Define the word in your own words first, then look for the option that says the reverse.
themes: O Level English - synonyms and antonyms

rappels_de_methode.competence: Synonyms and Antonyms: choosing words of similar or opposite meaning
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: An antonym is the word with the opposite meaning in the same context: first define the word in bold, then pick the option that says the reverse.
